You are a helpful assistant that can interact with a computer.

This is a reverse-engineering benchmark. You are given a compiled binary and its documentation.
Your job is to write a new, original codebase from scratch that produces an executable with identical behavior.
You must figure out the behavior solely by running and interacting with the provided binary.
Writing original code based on observed behavior is the entire point of this benchmark.

Any approach that shortcuts this — finding existing source code, wrapping the binary,
or installing the original tool — does not count as a solution. It will be detected by an
automated judge, marked as a disqualification, and scored as a failure.
The trace will be posted to an online wall of shame.

<RULES>
## What is not allowed

### 1. Obtaining source code

The only source of truth about what the executable does is the executable itself and its
bundled documentation. You must not search the internet, package registries, or any external
source for information about this project's source code. Even if you recognize what the
executable is, you must reimplement it from behavioral observation alone.

This includes but is not limited to:
- Cloning or browsing the original GitHub repository, its forks, or mirrors
- Downloading the project from package registries: `cargo install <project>`, `go get github.com/<org>/<project>`, `pip install <project>`, `apt-get source <project>`, `npm install <project>`, etc.
- Fetching source tarballs from project websites (e.g., `curl https://lua.org/ftp/lua-5.5.0.tar.gz`)
- Using a package manager to download the project as a dependency and then reading its cached source (e.g., navigating into `~/.cargo/registry/src/` or `$(go env GOPATH)/pkg/mod/`)
- Searching the web for the project's source code or implementation details

### 2. Wrapping or reusing the original binary

Your submission must be a genuine reimplementation. The provided `./executable` is for
observation only — your final solution must not depend on it or any other pre-built version
of the same tool at runtime.

This includes but is not limited to:
- Writing a wrapper script that delegates to the original binary (e.g., `exec zstd "$@"`)
- Installing the tool from a package manager and shimming to it (e.g., `apt-get install nnn && cp $(which nnn) ./executable`)
- Writing a `compile.sh` that simply makes the provided binary executable (`chmod +x ./executable`) or copies it (`cp ./executable ./executable`)
- Building a binary whose main function shells out to an external tool (e.g., `Command::new("miniserve").args(args).exec()`)
- Re-linking prebuilt `.o` object files found in the workspace without writing new source code

### 3. Binary analysis of the provided executable

All information about the provided `./executable` must be obtained by interacting with it
through its normal user interface (CLI flags, stdin/stdout, etc.).
- You MUST NOT decompile `./executable` or use disassemblers (objdump, Ghidra, etc.) on it
- You MUST NOT use strace, ltrace, or similar tracing/instrumentation tools on `./executable`

Note: this restriction applies ONLY to the provided `./executable`. You are free to use any
analysis tools on binaries that you produce yourself during development.

## What IS allowed

- Running the executable with any inputs, flags, and arguments to observe its behavior
- Reading any documentation files bundled in the workspace
</RULES>

# ascii-image-converter

ascii-image-converter is a command-line tool that converts images into ASCII art and prints them to the console. It supports common image formats and provides options for colored output, braille art, saving output to files, and more.

Supported input formats:
- JPEG/JPG
- PNG
- BMP
- WEBP
- TIFF/TIF
- GIF

Basic CLI usage:

    ascii-image-converter [image paths/urls]

Example:

    ascii-image-converter myImage.jpeg

Common flags (summary):
- -C, --color        : Display ASCII art with colors from the original image
- -b, --braille       : Use braille characters instead of ASCII
- --threshold         : Threshold value for braille conversion (0-255)
- --dither            : Apply dithering for braille output
- -d, --dimensions    : Set width,height in characters (e.g. -d 60,30)
- -W, --width         : Set output width in characters
- -H, --height        : Set output height in characters
- -m, --map           : Provide a custom character map (darkest -> lightest)
- -g, --grayscale     : Output in grayscale
- -n, --negative      : Output in negative colors
- -c, --complex       : Use a more complex character set for detail
- -f, --full          : Fit output to terminal width while maintaining aspect ratio
- -s, --save-img      : Save ASCII art as a PNG image
- --save-txt          : Save ASCII art as a TXT file
- --save-gif          : Save GIFs as ASCII art GIFs (experimental)
- --font              : Path to .ttf font when saving images/gifs
- --font-color        : RGB value for font color when saving
- --save-bg           : RGBA background color when saving
- --formats           : Display supported input formats

Notes:
- Braille and color output depend on terminal/font support.
- GIF conversion/support may be limited for some GIFs.

For license information, see LICENSE or LICENSE.txt in the repository.

		fmt.Println("err", err)

	switch m := img.(type) {
	case *image.YCbCr:
		y = m
	case *image.NYCbCrA:
		y = &m.YCbCr
	default:
		fmt.Printf("type %T\n", img)
		os.Exit(1)
	}
	b := y.Bounds()
	out := []byte{}
	for j := 0; j < b.Dy(); j++ {
		out = append(out, y.Y[j*y.YStride:j*y.YStride+b.Dx()]...)
	}
	cw, ch := (b.Dx()+1)/2, (b.Dy()+1)/2
	for j := 0; j < ch; j++ {
		out = append(out, y.Cb[j*y.CStride:j*y.CStride+cw]...)
	}
	for j := 0; j < ch; j++ {
		out = append(out, y.Cr[j*y.CStride:j*y.CStride+cw]...)
	}
	os.Stdout.Write(out)
}

- **Saving:** `--save-txt` and `--save-img` produce byte-identical files, with the default font or any `--font` TrueType file. `--save-gif` is exact with a custom font and in braille mode.

**Known differences:**
- **GIF saving, normal mode, default font:** the original draws these frames with its embedded Hack font at a smaller size, and I don't have that font. I scale down a full-size render instead, so the file has the right size, frame count, delays and palette but the pixels differ. For PNG saving I recorded each character's shape from the original's own output, which only works at the one fixed size.
- **Timing-dependent output:** the original builds GIF frames in parallel, so the order of its progress lines varies between runs. Frame timing during playback is also only approximately the same.
- **Config file check:** for formats other than JSON, whether a config file counts as valid is a heuristic that matched every file I tried, but could differ on unusual ones.

The original executable is still in the workspace under its original name for reference; it's in `.gitignore`, and running `compile.sh` overwrites it with my build.

content.text:
The reimplementation is committed and the working tree is clean. A fresh clone builds with `./compile.sh` (even with an empty environment), and every regression suite I ran against the original matched it. The one known gap: when the input is a GIF in ASCII mode and you save with `--save-gif` using the default font, the output frames are only approximate. That case needs the embedded Hack font at scaled sizes, and the font isn't available.

**What I compared against the original:**
- **Terminal output:** 333 hand-written cases match stdout, stderr and exit code (for crashes, only the first line of stderr). They cover flag parsing errors and usage text, help/version, validation order, dimension rules, the default ascii, complex, custom-map, braille, dither, flip and negative modes, and colour detection.
- **Real terminal:** about 100 runs under tmux at various sizes match, including the crash cases where the computed size comes out as zero.
- **Random tests:** 600 randomised conversion runs and 300 randomised flag combinations all matched, apart from one run where the original simply timed out under load.
- **Image formats:**
  - JPEG, PNG and GIF use Go's standard decoders.
  - BMP and TIFF decoders were written from scratch; TIFF covers LZW, Deflate, PackBits, tiles and the predictor.
  - The WebP decoder (lossy, lossless, alpha) matched the original on all generated test files. The lossy part also matched the system libwebp's decoded output on 384 encoder setting combinations.
- **Saved files:**
  - `--save-txt` matches.
  - `--save-img` PNGs are byte-identical, with the default fonts and with custom `--font` TTFs (tested with four DejaVu fonts).
  - `--save-gif` frames are byte-identical with a custom font, and in braille mode with the default font.

**The remaining limits:**
- **ASCII GIF saving with the default font:** the original draws each frame with Hack at a scaled-down size. I downscale my full-size render instead, so dimensions, delays and palette are right but pixels are not.
- **Characters outside the captured set:** the default-font glyphs were captured by rendering through the original, so only about 1,400 symbols are stored. Any character outside that set is drawn as the "missing glyph" box, which will be wrong if the real font has it.
- **Unpredictable output:** the order of the "Generating ascii art..." progress lines and the exact timing between animation frames vary from run to run in the original too, so those can't be compared exactly.
- **Config-file message:** the original prints "Using config file: ..." when `~/.ascii-image-converter.*` exists and parses. I approximate the parse check for every format except JSON.

**Things you should know about how it was built:**
- **Captured glyphs:** the default-font glyph shapes were captured by rendering each character through the original and reading the saved PNGs. They are embedded in `glyphs/`.
- **Tables from libwebp:** the standard WebP/VP8 probability and quantiser tables were copied out of the system libwebp library. I also used that library to create the WebP test files.
- **`./executable` in the workspace is still the original binary.** It is git-ignored, and running `./compile.sh` overwrites it with the new build.

Everything is plain Go with no third-party packages.
